description: Étudiant en 2e année à ELISA Aerospace, passionné par l'aéronautique et l'espace, je développe en Python et souhaite créer ASTRA LAB pour le NASA Space Apps Challenge. Je recherche des personnes motivées, notamment en développement web/mobile, création d'interfaces numériques, UX/UI design, IA et sciences spatiales, pour transformer cette idée en un prototype innovant.
summary:
Project name
ASTRA LAB – Astronaut health on a lunar base

High-level summary
ASTRA LAB is an interactive visual tool, built as a simulation game, in which an astronaut lives on a lunar base and has to monitor and maintain their own health. Health indicators are tracked continuously and shown with color coding (green / yellow / red): health, energy (fatigue), hydration, satiety, mental health (mood) and radiation exposure with cumulative dose in mSv. The astronaut is prompted to drink, eat, rest and sleep, can run a check-up at the infirmary scanner, take medicine or bandages, and take mental-health actions (call family, relax in the greenhouse, talk with a psychologist, play with the crew). Every action costs time and base resources (water, energy), as on a real mission. A companion robot (ASTRA GUIDE) explains each indicator, each risk and what to do, at three levels of detail. The tool is built around NASA’s five hazards of human spaceflight, so astronauts learn to assess themselves and act before a condition becomes critical.

Additional details
What it does. The astronaut walks through a lunar base (habitat, infirmary, greenhouse, water and oxygen room, power, EVA airlock, workshop, storage bay). A left-side panel always shows the clock and the health indicators with their values and colors. The top band summarizes the astronaut status and the bottom band the base systems (oxygen, water, power, radiation shielding, food).

How it maps to the five NASA hazards.
details:
Project name
ASTRA LAB – Astronaut health on a lunar base

High-level summary
ASTRA LAB is an interactive visual tool, built as a simulation game, in which an astronaut lives on a lunar base and has to monitor and maintain their own health. Health indicators are tracked continuously and shown with color coding (green / yellow / red): health, energy (fatigue), hydration, satiety, mental health (mood) and radiation exposure with cumulative dose in mSv. The astronaut is prompted to drink, eat, rest and sleep, can run a check-up at the infirmary scanner, take medicine or bandages, and take mental-health actions (call family, relax in the greenhouse, talk with a psychologist, play with the crew). Every action costs time and base resources (water, energy), as on a real mission. A companion robot (ASTRA GUIDE) explains each indicator, each risk and what to do, at three levels of detail. The tool is built around NASA’s five hazards of human spaceflight, so astronauts learn to assess themselves and act before a condition becomes critical.

Additional details
What it does. The astronaut walks through a lunar base (habitat, infirmary, greenhouse, water and oxygen room, power, EVA airlock, workshop, storage bay). A left-side panel always shows the clock and the health indicators with their values and colors. The top band summarizes the astronaut status and the bottom band the base systems (oxygen, water, power, radiation shielding, food).

How it maps to the five NASA hazards.

  • Space radiation: exposure (%) and cumulative dose (mSv) rise during rover sorties and solar storms, and fall inside the shielded base. Above 60 % exposure, health decreases.
  • Isolation and confinement: mood decreases over time. Below 25 %, stress causes fatigue and health loss. Countermeasures include family calls, a psychologist session every 3 days, crew games and messages from Earth every 14 days.
  • Distance from Earth: no resupply on demand. Medicine and bandages are limited (10 bandages per week), and water must be recycled or produced from lunar ice.
  • Gravity fields: daily exercise on the bike, with explanations about muscle and bone loss in low gravity.
  • Hostile closed environment: oxygen production, CO2 removal and water recycling are simulated hour by hour, and system failures affect the crew.

How it works. A shared simulation runs hour by hour (one in-game day = 2 minutes). Every action takes time and consumes resources, and the astronaut’s needs evolve with it: about -2.2 energy, -1.6 hydration and -1.2 satiety per hour awake. When health reaches zero, the suit’s survival system “reboots” the astronaut instead of a game over. Gamification is built in: experience points for completed tasks, levels, and 9 upgradable modules. A nightly report summarizes the astronaut’s health, and a progress bar tracks the mission.

Benefits. At-a-glance color-coded status, a routine of prompted actions, clear explanations (no prior medical knowledge assumed), and an engaging loop that rewards healthy behavior. It works fully offline.

What we hope to achieve. Next steps are to add vital-sign inputs (heart rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, body temperature, sleep hours), a clickable human figure, charts of indicators over time, and alerts for flight surgeons.

Tools. Python 3, pygame-ce, JSON saves, pytest (138 automated tests), ffmpeg for the demo video.

SI tools
Yes. We used a large language model (Claude, by Anthropic) as a coding and writing assistant: to help write and debug Python code, merge our three sub-teams’ code, generate tests, and draft documentation and this description. [Si c’est le cas : Some game artwork (room and mission backgrounds, start screen) was produced with an AI image generator.] The demo video carries a visible watermark: “Contains SI-generated imagery and SI-assisted code”. The project idea, the game design and the mapping to the spaceflight hazards are our own.

NASA data and resources used

  • NASA Human Research Program: the five hazards of human spaceflight (radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, hostile closed environments), used to choose and model the health indicators and countermeasures.
  • NASA ISS Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS): about 98 % water recovery and about 3.8 L of water per crew member per day, used for the water model.
  • NASA Apollo lunar sample data (382 kg returned by six missions) and NASA Artemis information on lunar south-pole water ice, used for rover sorties and ice-to-water production.
  • NASA Science – Moon (lunar gravity, day length, regolith), used for the base environment and the science cards.

All data, resources and tools
Python 3, pygame-ce (LGPL), pytest, ffmpeg. NASA sources: HRP hazards, ISS ECLSS water recovery (reported by Space.com, June 2023), Apollo lunar sample curation (NASA JSC, J. H. Allton), NASA Science – Moon, NASA Artemis. Claude (Anthropic) was used as a coding and writing assistant. All code and artwork were made by the team or with the SI tools stated above; no copyrighted third-party material is used.
